verses.translation_literal: To the Leader. Of the servant of YHWH, of David, who spoke to YHWH the words of this song on the day YHWH delivered him from the palm of all his enemies and from the hand of Saul.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster: a song of David, servant of the LORD. He spoke these words to the LORD on the day the LORD tore him free from the grip of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the title, and it is part of the poem: the Hebrew counts it as verse 1, which is why every later verse number is one higher than in the KJV. It tells the performers who sings and when: not in the thick of battle, but on a day of rescue remembered, the voice of someone safe at last. 'Servant of YHWH' is a title of honour in the ancient Near East, the word for a trusted royal officer; the poem opens by placing David in the position of the king's own servant before his divine king. The KJV turns 'of David' into 'A Psalm of David' and 'the servant of the Lord' into a plain apposition; the Hebrew gives only the bare genitives, with no word for 'psalm'. A pointed detail: David names 'all his enemies' and then Saul separately. Rashi, Radak and Meiri all read this as Saul weighing as much as all the rest together, the enemy who hunted him longest and from the inside. Note the literal 'palm' (kaf) for the enemies and 'hand' (yad) for Saul: the Hebrew varies the two words for a grasping hand, and most English versions flatten both to 'hand'.

philological_notes.note: The conventional heading 'to the choirmaster' or 'to the Leader'; the root נצח has to do with lasting, preeminence or leading. What it meant in practice (conductor, director of the temple music, or a tune title) is not settled.
Two words for 'hand': kaf, the palm or cupped hand that grasps, and yad. The change from 'palm' for the enemies to 'hand' for Saul is the poet's, and KJV levels both.
Saul is named after 'all his enemies' although he was one of them: Rashi says because he pressed hardest and pursued most; Radak and Meiri say he was weighed against all the others.

verses.translation_literal: And he said: I love you, YHWH, my strength.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he said, low and plain, before any image or any thunder: I love you, LORD, my strength.
verses.directors_commentary: The poem opens with a verb that appears nowhere else in this form: 'erchamkha. In the rest of the Bible rachum, 'merciful', belongs to the intensive stem and describes a superior pitying an inferior. Here a servant says it up to his king, in a stem that is not found elsewhere. The Targum, Rashi and Radak all translate it 'I love you', and the old versions agree, so the KJV's 'I will love thee' is acceptable except that it turns a present declaration into a promise; the Hebrew is a flat, spoken 'I love you'. The King's own word for the covenant bond is love, and a vassal who says it to his suzerain is speaking the language of treaty as well as of the heart. 'Strength' (chizqi) is a rare noun, also of the poem's own coinage, and sets the tone: the one who delivered is first named as source of power. Perform it quietly: this is the only line in the opening that is not about danger.

philological_notes.note: Qal of רחם, otherwise unattested; Rashi and Radak read it 'I love you' after the Aramaic translation of 'you shall love' (Lev 19:18). Ibn Ezra notes the root's other occurrences are in the intensive stem and gives 'I seek mercy from you' as an alternative. The vowel under the het is the rare short qamets.
'My strength': a noun from the root 'be strong', with a hireq under the het that Radak and Meiri remark on as unusual.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH [is] my crag and my stronghold and my deliverer, my God, my rock, I take refuge in him; my shield and the horn of my salvation, my refuge.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD is my cliff, my fortress, the one who lifts me out of danger. My God, my rock: in him I hide. My shield, the horn that saves me, my high place.
verses.directors_commentary: A run of ten titles for God, every one taken from a hunted man's landscape. David had lived it: Rashi on 'my crag' recalls the narrow place where Saul's men were closing round David and God rescued him (1 Sam 23:26), and Radak, commenting on 18:5, names it as the crag of the Divisions (1 Sam 23:28). Two words for rock appear: sela', a cleft cliff face, and tsur, a solid boulder, and the poet uses both. The KJV 'fortress', 'strength' and 'buckler' soften the picture. Verse 3b has 'my God, my rock', tsuri again, and the KJV renders it 'my strength' and so erases the repetition; 'buckler' is archaic for a small shield. 'Horn of my salvation' is the least obvious: the horn is the weapon and the pride of the wild ox, the animal whose horns make it strong, so Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David and Metzudat Zion read 'horn' as a symbol of power; it is not an altar horn or a trumpet. 'I take refuge' is chasah, the instinct of a creature running for cover, as under an overhang from the rain (Rashi on Job 24:8). The midrash cited by Radak counts ten titles against ten enemies of David, five from Israel and five from the nations. For performers: do not spread the titles evenly; they come faster and faster, like a man naming every piece of cover he can see.

philological_notes.note: Two words for rock: sela' (a cliff or crag, a place to climb to) and tsur (a boulder or mass of rock, also a name of God). Rashi glosses tsuri as 'sela' ' and Metzudat Zion as strength like a rock.
'Horn of my salvation': horn as a figure of strength, from the ox or ram, whose horns are its weapon. The Hebrew uses the horn as a figure of power, not as a musical instrument.
'I take refuge': the creature's taking cover. Rashi compares Job 24:8, where rocks shelter travellers from wind and rain.

verses.translation_literal: Praised, I call out [to] YHWH, and from my enemies I am saved.
verses.translation_dramatic: Praised be he: that is the name I cry to the LORD by, and from my enemies I am saved.
verses.directors_commentary: The grammar of the opening word is the puzzle. Mehullal is a passive participle, 'praised' or 'to be praised'. It can describe God ('I call on YHWH, who is worthy of praise', KJV and ASV), or it can name how David calls ('I call, praising'). The Hebrew puts it first, before the verb, as if it were a title: YLT's 'The Praised One I call Jehovah' keeps that force. Rashi and Meiri take it as the manner of the call: David praises before he is saved, because he is sure of the outcome. Malbim, in a more elaborate scheme, reads it as the voice of a man not yet in distress. The KJV's 'so shall I be saved' adds a result ('so') the Hebrew does not state; there is only 'and', and the verb is a passive 'I am saved' that leaves rescue as simple fact rather than consequence. Play it as faith spoken before the proof.

philological_notes.note: A passive participle, 'praised', set before the verb: either God's epithet or the manner of David's calling. Rashi: David praises before he is delivered, sure that he will be.
Niphal, 'I am saved': a completed rescue stated plainly, not a conditional result as in KJV 'so shall I be'.

verses.translation_literal: The cords of death encompassed me, and the torrents of worthlessness terrified me.
verses.translation_dramatic: They closed around me, the ropes of death, and the floods of ruin came roaring down and filled me with dread.
verses.directors_commentary: Two pictures of drowning and binding. Chevel means a rope or a cord, and also the pangs of a woman in labour: the pull of a rope and the pull of pain are the same word. Ibn Ezra notes that the vowel on chevlei separates it from the 'allotment' in Joshua 17:5, and Rashi, Radak and Metzudat Zion cite labour pains (Hosea 13:13). The KJV's 'sorrows of death' keeps only the pain and loses the rope. The other image is nachalei, 'wadis' or 'torrents': in this country a dry gully that fills in minutes when it rains in the hills, and that kills people who are standing in it. Rashi and Radak read it as troops or troubles sweeping in like a torrent. 'Beliya'al' is worthlessness, a word the Bible uses for the lawless and later as a name for evil itself; KJV 'ungodly men' fixes it as people, which the Hebrew leaves open. The etymology is itself debated: Metzudat Zion derives it from bli 'ol, 'without a yoke', the lawless who threw off heaven's yoke, while Radak says it names each enemy or is the name of the wicked one. Radak and Meiri also hear nachalei as 'sicknesses', from nachalah in Jeremiah 30:12, so that the line would say blows rather than floods. The sound matters too: 'afafuni and yeva'atuni echo, a closing circle of sound.

philological_notes.note: Rope or cord, and also birth pangs (Hos 13:13). Metzudat Zion gives 'pains', Rashi 'bands' of enemies, and Targum Jonathan reads a woman on the birth-stool.

'Torrents of worthlessness': wadis in flood as a figure for overwhelming enemies. The etymology of beliya'al is debated: Metzudat Zion derives it from 'without yoke' (bli 'ol), the lawless who threw off heaven's yoke; Radak allows each enemy or a proper name; Radak and Meiri also give nachalei as 'sicknesses' (Jer 30:12).

verses.translation_literal: The cords of Sheol surrounded me; the snares of death confronted me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The ropes of Sheol wound round me. The snares of death were there before me, waiting.
verses.directors_commentary: The poet repeats his picture at a lower depth: from death to Sheol, from cords to traps. Sheol is the place of the dead beneath the earth, the pit where all go; the KJV's 'hell' is a mistranslation, since the Hebrew knows nothing of a place of punishment, only of the grave and the silence below. 'Prevented me' in the KJV is its archaic 'came before me' (Latin praevenire): the Hebrew qiddemuni means they met me head-on, 'came in front of me', and a modern reader will take 'prevented' to mean the opposite. Moqesh is a bird-trap, a snare set on the ground: death is the hunter and David the bird. Two words for 'surround', two for 'trap': the verse is built as a net, and should be spoken with the same closing pace.

philological_notes.note: Sheol, the underworld, the realm of the dead; not 'hell' as KJV renders it. Radak and Rashi, following the Aramaic of 2 Sam 22:6, also read it as a company of the wicked.
Piel of 'to be in front': they came upon me or confronted me. KJV 'prevented' is its older sense 'anticipated', which now misleads. Metzudat Zion: 'they came before me'.
Snares or traps laid for birds; the figure is a hunter and its prey.

verses.translation_literal: In the distress to me I call [to] YHWH, and to my God I cry for help; he hears from his temple my voice, and my cry for help before him comes in his ears.
verses.translation_dramatic: In my narrow place I called on the LORD, and to my God I cried for help. And from his temple he heard my voice; my cry went before him and came into his very ears.
verses.directors_commentary: The turn of the poem. Tsar is the 'tight place', the word that gives 'distress' (Hebrew 'narrowness'): a man pinned in a gap with the ropes round him. The verbs are in the imperfect, which can be 'I called' or 'I call'; the KJV's past tense is one fair choice, YLT's present another. Note the doubled line: 'I call' and 'I cry for help' (qara' and shiva'), then 'my voice' and 'my cry', then 'before him' and 'in his ears'. Metzudat David says the repetition is the habit of poetry, nothing more. 'His temple' (heikhal) is the royal hall, the great room of a palace, and it is also the word for the temple; Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take it as heaven, which is where the decrees are kept. The surprise is the movement of a cry in three steps: from the mouth, to the presence, to the ear. The cry does not simply rise; it is delivered. Audiences in a world of kings who were never reached by petitioners would feel the daring of 'into his ears'.

philological_notes.note: 'His temple', or 'his palace': a great hall, used both for a king's palace and for the sanctuary. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri take it to mean heaven.
To cry out for help (Piel); a more urgent cry than 'to call' and the root of the noun shav'ati in the second line.

verses.translation_literal: And the earth shook and quaked, and the foundations of the mountains trembled, and they shook back and forth, for it burned to him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the earth heaved and shuddered. The roots of the mountains shook, rocked, and reeled, because his anger had caught fire.
verses.directors_commentary: The theophany, the appearance of God in storm and earthquake, begins here, and it has the sound of an earthquake: va-tig'ash va-tir'ash, two verbs that rhyme and rattle. English can only borrow: 'shook and quaked'. The 'foundations of the mountains' are the mooring posts that ancient cosmology gave the earth, the pillars under it; to move them is to threaten creation itself. The last clause is the hardest for the KJV, which gives 'because he was wroth', a stately and abstract phrase. Hebrew says charah lo, 'it burned to him', the idiom for anger, the same heat that comes next in verse 9 as smoke from the nose. So the anger is physical and is already moving toward the fire. Rashi reads the verse as the end of a sentence begun earlier and the 'for' as 'when'; Ibn Ezra and Meiri say the quake is a figure for the enemies' panic, though the old commentators disagree on whether it recalls the Exodus or the fall of David's enemies. The rescue of a single man is staged as a cosmic upheaval: there is no proportion, and that is the point.

philological_notes.note: A rhyming pair of verbs for the earth's shaking. Metzudat Zion compares the surging of rivers in Jeremiah 46:7 for the first.
Literally 'it burned to him', the usual idiom for anger; KJV's 'was wroth' loses the heat that the next verse develops as smoke and fire.

token_glosses.gloss: and they shook back and forth

verses.translation_literal: Smoke went up in his nose, and fire from his mouth consumed; coals burned from him.
verses.translation_dramatic: Smoke rose from his nostrils; fire poured from his mouth and ate whatever it touched. Coals blazed up from him.
verses.directors_commentary: God is pictured as a furious creature, a bull or a dragon that snorts smoke and breathes fire. 'Af is both 'nose' and 'anger', so 'smoke in his nose' says in one phrase that he is angry and that he is burning; the KJV's 'out of his nostrils' is correct as a body part but hides that the same word means wrath. Rashi observes that this is simply what anger does (it sends smoke from the nostrils) and Metzudat Zion compares 'Why does your anger smoke?' (Ps 74:1). The fire 'eats': the Hebrew verb is the same as for a meal, so the flames feed. Malbim reads the whole scene as a volcano; other commentators as a figure for judgment. Ugarit and Egypt have such images for their storm gods; the poem gives them to the one God. Speak it low and fast; every phrase is the next stage of heat.

philological_notes.note: 'In his nose' and 'in his anger': af means both. Metzudat Zion and Rashi take the smoke as the visible sign of anger.
'Consumed', literally 'ate': the fire eats like an animal.

verses.translation_literal: And he bent the heavens and came down, and thick darkness [was] under his feet.
verses.translation_dramatic: He bent the heavens down and descended, and under his feet lay a darkness so thick it could be touched.
verses.directors_commentary: Here the poet draws the sky as a tent or a dome that God presses down as he steps through it, as a king might lower a curtain. 'Arafel is not the KJV's plain 'darkness' but a heavy, low cloud, the storm cloud that hid Sinai (Ex 20:21; Deut 4:11); the word suggests something thick enough to be stood on, which is what 'under his feet' says. The KJV also has 'was under', which smooths the sudden nominal clause: after two quick verbs the Hebrew simply names the darkness, a held beat. Rashi says the descent is for the crossing of Egypt, Metzudat David that it is a figure of speed, Ibn Ezra that the decree falls from heaven on the enemy. A theophany in this tradition is always partly hidden: God arrives, and no one sees him.

philological_notes.note: Thick, low cloud and dark, the storm cloud of Sinai; Metzudat Zion glosses it 'the gloom of cloud'.
'He bent the heavens': the sky is lowered like a tent so God can come down. Metzudat David reads it as hurrying to repay the enemies.

verses.translation_literal: And he rode on a cherub and flew, and he soared on the wings of the wind.
verses.translation_dramatic: He mounted a cherub and flew; he swooped upon the wings of the wind.
verses.directors_commentary: A storm god rides a cloud-chariot: Ugarit says it of Baal, and the Bible says it of YHWH with a difference. Here the vehicle is a cherub, which was not a chubby child but a winged guardian, part lion, part eagle, part human, that stood at palace doors and bore thrones; in the temple two cherubim flanked the ark, the throne of the invisible God. To 'ride a cherub' is to be a king on his throne in motion. The KJV 'did fly: yea, he did fly' flattens two different verbs into one repeated 'fly' and adds a 'yea' the Hebrew does not have. The Hebrew has three rapid verbs: 'rode' (vayirkav), 'flew' (vaya'of, the common verb for any winged creature) and 'soared' (vayede', a rarer verb for an eagle swooping on its prey, Deut 28:49). The poet climbs from the common verb to the rare one, and a translation that repeats 'fly' loses the climb. The ASV's 'soared' keeps the difference, though it too keeps the 'yea'. BBE's 'seated on a storm-cloud' explains the picture and removes it. Metzudat Zion identifies the cherub with an angel; Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David read the ride as speed. For performers: the line gets lighter and faster, as if the verse itself is taking off.

philological_notes.note: A cherub, a winged composite guardian of thrones and sacred places; not the child-angel of later art. Metzudat Zion calls it an angel.

Two different verbs for flight: ʿuf, 'to fly' (any winged creature), and daʾah, 'to soar, swoop', the verb for an eagle in Deut 28:49. Rashi and Meiri gloss vayede' as vaya'of and cite Deut 28:49; Metzudat Zion cites the same verse. KJV levels both to 'fly'.

verses.translation_literal: He made darkness his covering; around him his canopy, darkness of waters, dark clouds of the skies.
verses.translation_dramatic: He wrapped himself in darkness and hid; the tent he pitched around him was black water, storm-heavy clouds across the sky.
verses.directors_commentary: God conceals himself. The word sitro, 'his hiding place' or 'covering', is the place of concealment, and it is joined to sukkato, 'his booth', the same word as the leafy shelter of the festival of Sukkot or a soldier's field hut. The Almighty in his tent is a king on campaign, and the tent is made of storm. The KJV's 'pavilion' is a fair old word for a great tent, but 'secret place' and 'dark waters and thick clouds' break the Hebrew's piled-up nouns: 'cheshkhat mayim', 'darkness of waters', is a phrase with no verb, only stacking, one dark on another, and 'avei shechaqim' is the thickness of the clouds. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Meiri tie this to a sky heavy with water: Ibn Ezra explains the darkness as vapour rising thick; Meiri notes 2 Samuel 22:12 has a different word for 'gathering' there. Staging note: the divine presence is both shown and hidden. The scene should go dark, not bright.

philological_notes.note: His hiding place or covering. God is concealed in the darkness, not revealed by light.
'His booth' or canopy: the word of the festival shelter and the soldier's hut, here the tent of the divine king.

'Darkness of waters'. The parallel in 2 Samuel 22:12 has a different word, chashrat; Meiri takes it as a binding together of clouds. Metzudat David: the darkness comes from the masses of water held in the clouds.

verses.translation_literal: From the brightness before him his dark clouds passed on — hail and coals of fire.
verses.translation_dramatic: Out of the radiance that burns before him the storm clouds roll, heavy and black, and from their bellies fall hail like struck stones and embers still glowing.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the poem turns from the earthquake and smoke of the earlier verses to a full thunderstorm, and the actors must hear the contrast: brightness (נֹגַהּ) in front of God, darkness (עָבִים) around him, and out of the dark comes the weapon. The Hebrew order is stark: 'from brightness before him, his clouds passed — hail and coals of fire.' The last four words are not a sentence but a flash, with no verb, as if the speaker simply points. In Israel's world the storm is the weapon of the divine warrior. The neighbouring Baal of Ugarit rides the clouds and flings thunder; this psalm gives that role to YHWH alone, and that is part of its polemic. Hail and lightning-fire together recall the plague of Exod 9:24, which the sages heard behind the verse (Rashi on Psalm 18:13 sets it at the Red Sea).

The KJV 'thick clouds' is acceptable for עָב, and 'at the brightness' for מִן, though the preposition says 'out of', so the light is the source and not the occasion. The KJV also inserts 'hail stones', where the Hebrew has the plain mass noun 'hail'. 'Coals' is the word for burning embers (גַּחֲלֵי), not the later English 'live coals' of metaphor: this is fire that falls.

philological_notes.note: The verb is 'pass over, cross, sweep on', the same root as the crossing of the sea, so the clouds are an army on the march. Ibn Ezra hears in it the clouds passing beyond their usual law ('exceeding the known rule in abundance'); Metzudat David takes it as the clouds carrying the hail across to the enemy.
Brightness, shining light; it is the glow that precedes the lightning, not the flash itself. Meiri hears it as the merit of the righteous, a moral reading beside the meteorological one.

verses.translation_literal: And he thundered in the heavens, YHWH, and the Most High gave his voice — hail and coals of fire.
verses.translation_dramatic: Then the LORD thunders from the heavens. The Most High lifts his voice, and the whole sky answers it with hail and with embers of fire.
verses.directors_commentary:
The refrain 'hail and coals of fire' returns word for word from the last verse, and the director should let it fall twice, like a second peal after the first. Hebrew poetry often does this with a stock line, and Ibn Ezra notes that the repetition joins the two things into a single moment. Now the thunder is the voice: קוֹל, the same word used throughout the ancient world for the storm god's speech (compare Psalm 29, 'the voice of YHWH', seven times). The poet gives the thunder to YHWH and to the Most High (עֶלְיוֹן) together, the second name an old title of God that is also used for Canaanite El; the verse puts both on one speaker, and the audience hears no rival.

The KJV 'also thundered' adds a word, 'also', that is not there: the Hebrew begins with a plain 'and he thundered'. The word order is marked, since the divine name comes late, after the verb and 'in the heavens', so that the name arrives like the clap itself. The KJV 'the Highest' is sound; 'gave his voice' is the idiom that keeps the Hebrew נָתַן קוֹל, 'to give out voice', and English 'uttered' (ASV) flattens it.

philological_notes.note: The verb is the hiphil of the root for thunder: 'he caused to thunder', and with God as subject it means he acts through the storm. The noun רַעַם is the thunder itself; Ibn Ezra notes the root as the base of the verb.
'Most High', an old divine epithet; here it stands parallel to YHWH, so one God has two names. The STEPBible entity link joins it to YHWH.

verses.translation_literal: And he sent out his arrows and scattered them, and lightning flashes he shot, and routed them.
verses.translation_dramatic: He looses his arrows, and the enemy scatters like chaff. He shoots the lightning, bolt on bolt, and they break and run in panic.
verses.directors_commentary:
The storm is now an archery duel. Lightning is God's arrow (חֵץ), and his enemies are the target. The poet has the verbs arrive in a quick chain, 'sent… scattered… shot… routed', and the actors should play them as four blows. This is the language of the warrior god: the Ugaritic storm god has bolts, and Habakkuk 3:11 says 'at the light of your arrows as they flew'. The psalm borrows the picture and gives the arsenal to YHWH.

Two words are lost in the KJV. First, וַיְהֻמֵּם is not 'discomfited', a courtly word for embarrassed, but 'he threw them into panic': the root הָמַם is the one used of the confusion God sends on an army (it is the holy-war word of the Red Sea). Second, רָב. The KJV 'he shot out lightnings' follows the old reading of רבב as a verb 'to shoot', which Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Radak defend by a parallel with Gen 49:23, where the archers 'shot at' Joseph. The ASV and YLT, who read 'lightnings manifold', treat it as the adjective 'many'. Both are possible; the verb gives a better line, because it pairs with 'sent'.

philological_notes.note: 'He threw them into confusion', 'routed': it is the panic that breaks an army's formation before any blow lands. KJV 'discomfited' is the old sense of 'defeated', which modern readers do not hear.

Read as a perfect verb 'he shot (arrows)', from the geminate root רבב. Ibn Ezra, Meiri and Radak cite the shape of the root, and Metzudat Zion links it to 'archer' (רֹבֶה קַשָּׁת, Gen 21:20). Malbim reads the arrows as lightning bolts whose abundance silences the thunder.

verses.translation_literal: And the channels of water were seen, and the foundations of the world were uncovered, from your rebuke, YHWH, from the breath of the wind of your nose.
verses.translation_dramatic: And the sea floor stands bare. The channels of the deep lie open to the light, and the very foundations of the world are laid naked, at your rebuke, O LORD, at the gust that rushes from your nostrils.
verses.directors_commentary:
From sky to abyss. The storm now strikes the waters under the earth, and the ancient audience, who thought the world sat on pillars set in a primeval sea, would feel the floor drop away. 'Channels' (אֲפִיקִים) are the beds of streams or the gullies of the sea; 'foundations of the world' (מוֹסְדוֹת תֵּבֵל) are the supports of the earth's disc. The picture is of the waters driven back, as at creation and at the Red Sea. Rashi hears the Exodus here, and Radak lists the Sea of Reeds and the Jordan as the old readings.

The agent is 'your rebuke' (גְּעָרָה), the word used when God drives back the sea in Psalm 104:7 and 106:9, and Radak cites 106:9, 'he rebuked the sea and it dried'. God's shout is enough. Then comes the body: 'the breath of the wind of your nose'. The KJV 'blast of the breath of thy nostrils' is accurate but smooths a pile of words: נִשְׁמַת (breath), רוּחַ (wind or spirit) and אַף (nose, and by extension anger). Every word means breath; the pile is the gust. The Hebrew speaks of God's nose and so of his anger at once, and the director should let the actors flare a nostril.

philological_notes.note: 'Rebuke', the sharp speech that makes the sea flee; it is the verb of the divine warrior against chaos (Ps 104:7, 106:9). Radak cites the second.
'Channels of water': a gully or watercourse, which Meiri says becomes visible when the flood drains. Metzudat David reads it as the bed of the waters laid bare when they are split.
Three words for breath piled up, with 'nose/anger' last. Rashi glosses נִשְׁמַת as 'blowing'. Metzudat David says the whole is a figure.

verses.translation_literal: He sends from on high, he takes me, he draws me out of many waters.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then, from the height, a hand reaches down. It takes hold of me. It draws me up out of the deep, out of the great and drowning waters.
verses.directors_commentary:
The cosmic storm narrows to one man. After eleven verses of thunder, the psalm shifts to a single gesture, a reaching hand, and the actors should drop their voices. The Hebrew is spare: 'sends', 'takes', 'draws', each a plain verb with 'me' on the end of the last two. The 'many waters' (מַיִם רַבִּים) are the flood of the opening of the psalm (the 'torrents of Belial', v.5) and, in the ancient imagination, the realm of death.

The verb יַמְשֵׁנִי is the one that matters. It is the verb behind the name Moses (מֹשֶׁה): Pharaoh's daughter says 'I drew him out of the water' (Exod 2:10), and Rashi on this verse points to that very passage. A listener who knew Israel's story would hear that the speaker, drawn from the water like the first rescued child, is a new Moses. The KJV 'he drew me out' keeps the verb but loses the echo, because nothing in English ties it to Moses. The verb 'took' (יִקָּחֵנִי) is also stronger than it looks: it is the word for seizing, as God 'took' Enoch.

philological_notes.note: 'He draws me out (of water)'. Same root as the name Moses; Rashi quotes Exod 2:10 and Metzudat Zion does too. The sound is that of the later rescued leader.
'From the height', the heavens as the place of God's throne; Ibn Ezra and Rashi take it as God's messengers coming down, though the Hebrew has none.

verses.translation_literal: He rescues me from my enemy, strong, and from those hating me, for they [were] too strong for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: He pulled me clear of the enemy who was strong, stronger than I, and of every one of those who hated me. I could not have stood against them. They were too strong for me, and still I was drawn out.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the pivot of the rescue story: after the storm and the hand from on high, the king says plainly what he was saved from. Play it as a confession, not a boast. He was not a hero who won; he was a man who was outmatched, and the line ends on the word 'for me', the weakest word in the verse.

The singular 'my enemy, strong' beside the plural 'those hating me' puzzles the commentators. Radak reads the singular as a single champion, Goliath or Ishbi-benob (the giant of 2 Sam 21:16); Meiri reads it as Saul. Ibn Ezra hears the water image still running underneath, as the enemy is the flood, and notes that a word is missing from the Hebrew. The KJV 'delivered' is fair, but it turns a Hebrew imperfect into a flat past and hides the habitual note that the psalm has been building: this is what this God does. The two words for strength differ (עָז, then אָמְצוּ), and English 'strong' and 'too strong' flatten both into one.

philological_notes.note: Literally 'my enemy, strong': a singular noun with an adjective, set against the plural 'those hating me'. Radak reads the singular as one champion, Goliath or Ishbi-benob (2 Sam 21:16); Meiri reads it as Saul. Ibn Ezra notes that a word is missing and ties the line to the water image of the preceding verses.

'They were strong, they prevailed'. With מִן 'from' it means 'too strong for' (stronger than). Metzudat David reads it as a time clause: when they grew strong against me in battle, then he rescued me.

token_glosses.gloss: and from those who hate me

verses.translation_literal: They confront me in the day of my calamity, and YHWH becomes a support for me.
verses.translation_dramatic: They came at me on the day my ground gave way. But the LORD was there, a staff to lean on when my own legs would not hold.
verses.directors_commentary:
'The day of my calamity' (יוֹם אֵידִי) is a known term for the day disaster falls, the day the enemy knows to strike. Rashi says the enemies hurried to get there first; Metzudat David adds their cruel reckoning: when a man begins to fall, they thought, he would not rise again. The verb יְקַדְּמוּנִי is the heart of this. It means 'they came to meet me, ahead of me', so the enemy is waiting at the gate of the man's worst day. The KJV 'prevented me' is Elizabethan English: 'prevent' once meant 'go before' (Latin praevenire), and a modern reader takes it to mean the opposite, 'stopped'. The Hebrew is of an ambush, not a blocking.

Then the turn. The word מִשְׁעָן is a staff or prop, the thing a man leans his weight on; the Hebrew says 'YHWH became to me for a support', and the verb 'became' (וַיְהִי) marks a turn: on that day he took the part of a support. The KJV 'stay' is the same archaic sense of a prop.

philological_notes.note: 'They come before me, they meet me ahead of time'. Rashi: the enemies hurried and came early to the day of his calamity. KJV 'prevented' is its older English equivalent.
Calamity, ruin, the sudden blow. Metzudat Zion links it to Job 31:3, and the Targum glosses it as exile or wandering.
A support to lean on: staff, prop. The root is the lean of a man on his stick.

verses.translation_literal: And he brings me out to the broad place; he rescues me, for he delights in me.
verses.translation_dramatic: He led me out into open country, where the walls were gone and the air was wide, and he set me free. Why? Because he took delight in me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the opposite of the verse where the psalm began: 'in my distress (בַּצַּר לִי) I called' (v.7), and now God brings the speaker out to the 'broad place' (מֶרְחָב). Ibn Ezra notes the reversal. Tight and wide are the poem's pair, as a mountain pass against open plain, a besieged town against open field. The word צַר (narrow) is also the word for 'enemy', so being brought into the wide place means leaving both.

The verb יְחַלְּצֵנִי means to draw out, to strip off, to pull a man from what holds him, as one pulls off a sandal (Deut 25:9, the same root). It is more physical than 'delivered' (KJV), which has gone abstract and legal in modern English. And the last clause is the one the psalm will not explain: כִּי חָפֵץ בִּי, 'because he took pleasure in me'. The KJV 'delighted in me' is right. There is no reason given beyond God's will, which is why the next verses, which claim merit, can seem to be in tension with this one. The director should let the actors notice it.

philological_notes.note: 'Roomy place', broad open space, the opposite of the narrowness of distress. Metzudat David: a wide place in which to escape their hands. Ibn Ezra reads it as the reverse of 'in my distress I called'.
'He delights in me, he wants me': the cause of the rescue is God's own pleasure.

verses.translation_literal: YHWH deals with me according to my righteousness; according to the cleanness of my hands he returns to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD deals with me as my righteousness deserves. As clean as my hands have been, so he gives back to me.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the speaker makes a claim, and the actors should not rush it. In a world where kings were judged by their gods, this is the royal innocence formula: 'my righteousness', 'the cleanness of my hands'. It is not boasting, since the claim is about a specific accusation, as when David spares Saul. Rashi ties the first to David cutting Saul's cloak rather than killing him (1 Sam 24:4), and Radak says the speaker knew that right was with him and wrong with his enemies.

The Hebrew uses two verbs, גָּמַל (to deal with, to give what is due, the verb of weaning and of repayment) and הֵשִׁיב (to return, to pay back), and the KJV smooths them into 'rewarded' and 'recompensed'. Malbim sees a difference: one is the payment fitted to the act, the other fitted to the love behind it. The word בֹּר (cleanness) is rare. Hands are the instrument of action, so clean hands are a clean record. Ibn Ezra notes that since most deeds are done by hands, the poet puts them in.

philological_notes.note: 'He deals with me, he requites': the verb is used for repayment in either direction and the sense is set by the object. Malbim distinguishes it from הֵשִׁיב as payment of love against payment of deed.
'Cleanness of my hands', related to בַּר לֵבָב, 'pure of heart' (Ps 24:4), as Rashi says. The sense is of being free of guilt, above all of blood.

verses.translation_literal: For I have kept the ways of YHWH, and I have not acted wickedly from my God.
verses.translation_dramatic: For I have walked in the ways of the LORD and kept them. I have not turned wicked and gone from my God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker gives the ground of the claim. 'The ways of YHWH' (דַּרְכֵי יְהוָה) is the language of covenant life as a road, and 'kept' (שָׁמַרְתִּי) is the verb of a sentry, who guards a thing that could be lost. Ibn Ezra splits the two halves in a way a director can use: 'kept' is the commandments one must do, 'not acted wickedly' the ones one must not. The second clause, וְלֹא רָשַׁעְתִּי מֵאֱלֹהָי, is odd Hebrew, since 'I have not been wicked from my God' joins a verb of guilt to a preposition of departing. The KJV 'wickedly departed' resolves it, and so do the others, and it is a fair rendering. The literal layer keeps the oddness: wickedness here is a moving away.

Radak adds a second reading, which sits well with the story of David and Saul: the speaker was hunted and could have killed the king, and did not, since Saul was the LORD's anointed (1 Sam 26:9). The speaker is protesting innocence of the specific charge, not of every sin; elsewhere the Psalms are well aware of sin. KJV 'the Lord' for YHWH hides the name that the Hebrew puts first, in the same verse as 'my God', the personal and the covenant name side by side.

philological_notes.note: 'I have been wicked (away) from my God'. The verb is the root of 'wicked' (רָשָׁע), here with מִן of separation. Radak: not deliberately and wilfully leaving the path, save by error; Meiri hears also a claim not to have spoken wrongly about God; Metzudat David glosses 'from the commandments of my God'.
'I have kept, guarded': the sentry's verb; Ibn Ezra takes it as keeping the positive commandments.

verses.translation_literal: For all his judgments are before me, and his statutes I do not remove from me.
verses.translation_dramatic: For all his judgments stood before my eyes, and his statutes I never put away from me.
verses.directors_commentary:
The two words for law, מִשְׁפָּטִים (judgments, decisions) and חֻקּוֹת (statutes, things engraved), cover the whole of God's instruction, and the poet sets them in two places: 'before me' and 'not removed from me'. The first is a thing seen at a distance, a document held up before the eyes; the second is a thing worn, on the body. Malbim reads the contrast as one between laws reason would demand and laws received without a reason. The director can play it more simply: one is in front, one is close.

The verb אָסִיר is the hiphil of סוּר, 'to turn aside', and so 'to remove': it is what one does with a garment or a ring. The KJV 'put away' is good. The KJV 'were before me' puts the first clause in the past; the Hebrew has no verb at all (לְנֶגְדִּי, 'before me'), and the verb of the second is an imperfect, so the whole stays in a timeless present of habit: this is what the speaker always does. The king of Israel was to keep his own copy of the law with him and read it all his days (Deut 17:18-19), and the claim has a royal ring.

philological_notes.note: 'Before me, in front of me', in sight. Rashi: 'I always set them before my eyes'; Radak: I never forgot them.
'Judgments' and 'statutes'. Malbim distinguishes the first as what reason requires and the second as what is received without a reason; Meiri reads them as the rational and the revealed teachings.

verses.translation_literal: And I was blameless with him, and I kept myself from my iniquity.
verses.translation_dramatic: I stood whole before him. And I guarded myself against the wrong that was my own.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker closes the claim with two verbs. The first is 'I was blameless with him' (תָּמִים עִמּוֹ), and the director should hear the preposition: not 'before him' (KJV 'upright before him'), but 'with him', beside him, in his company. תָּמִים is not sinless but whole, complete, undivided, and it is the word used of sacrificial animals that have no defect. The KJV 'upright' and the ASV 'perfect' each take one half of it: upright suggests moral posture, perfect suggests a flawless result, and the Hebrew means a whole thing, with nothing missing.

The second verb is reflexive: וָאֶשְׁתַּמֵּר, 'I kept myself', so the speaker is his own sentry. The last phrase, מֵעֲוֹנִי, is 'from my iniquity', and the possessive is the point. Meiri says it means the sin to which he was prone, the one that belonged to him. That is a humbler claim than the sweeping ones before it: the speaker does not say he had no failing, only that he guarded the one he knew. The KJV 'mine iniquity' is archaic in form but right in sense.

philological_notes.note: 'Whole, blameless, complete'. Used for animals fit for the altar, and for a person whose heart is not divided. Ibn Ezra glosses it with the phrase 'you shall be blameless' (תָּמִים תִּהְיֶה).
Hithpael of 'keep': 'I guarded myself'. Meiri reads 'my iniquity' as the one to which a man is prone; Metzudat David glosses it as what counted as sin for me.

verses.translation_literal: And YHWH returned to me according to my righteousness, according to the cleanness of my hands before his eyes.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so the LORD has paid me back, measure for measure, in the coin of my own righteousness. My hands were clean, and he saw them clean: they were held up in front of his eyes, and nothing in them was hidden.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse closes the long claim of innocence that began at verse 21 and states its payoff: the king reads his rescue as a verdict. The verb is the same one used for repaying a debt or returning a loan, and the language is the language of the law court. 'Cleanness of my hands' is an image of the courtroom, where open, washed hands show that no blood or bribe has stuck to them. Play it quiet. This is a man who knows how it sounds to say 'I was righteous', and the closing words 'before his eyes' keep it from boasting: the judge is the one who counts, not the crowd (Metzudat David on 18:25: 'not before human beings, to be proud').

KJV 'recompensed' and 'in his eyesight' are fair, but 'Therefore' is added by the translators, and it hides that the Hebrew has a plain 'And' that follows on from the narrative of rescue. KJV also writes 'the Lord' where the Hebrew has the name YHWH, which makes it sound like a title rather than a personal name.

philological_notes.note: 'Cleanness, purity': from the root meaning to sort out or make clear. It is a rare noun, which appears again in Job 22:30 and 2 Sam 22:21, and it is the base of the verb in verse 27 (titbarar), so the speaker's purity is answered by God's purity. Radak ties the two together at verse 27.

'In front of his eyes', a legal posture: the evidence is laid before the judge. Ibn Ezra connects it with 'all his judgments are before me' (Ps 18:23), so the two verses form a frame around the king's plea.

verses.translation_literal: With a faithful one you show yourself faithful; with a man, blameless, you show yourself blameless;
verses.translation_dramatic: With the faithful, you show yourself faithful. With the man who is whole, you show yourself whole.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the psalm leaves the story of the rescue and turns to the one it has been speaking to, in the second person: 'you'. The voice should drop and slow. It is a principle, almost a proverb, and it comes out of what the king has just said about his own clean hands.

The Hebrew is built as a mirror: the same root on each side of the verb, 'a faithful one (chasid), you show yourself faithful (titchasad)', 'a blameless man (tamim), you show yourself blameless (titamam)'. Both verbs are reflexive-stem forms: God is said to display or act out the quality he meets. Meiri takes the stem as one of intensity, 'you show your faithfulness strongly'. Radak adds that God repays the faithful even more than they deserve. The KJV 'merciful' for chasid shrinks a covenant word, loyalty within a bond, into pity, and 'upright' for tamim loses 'whole, complete, without remainder'. The unusual word for 'man' is gever, not the usual ish; Ibn Ezra says it is an adjective in form, not a construct, and Radak and Metzudat Zion read it simply as 'man'. Rashi finds the three fathers in the three words, and the Targum applies the verse to Abraham and Isaac.

philological_notes.note: A reflexive-stem verb from the same root as חָסִיד: 'you show yourself faithful'. Meiri reads the stem as strengthening the action, 'you show your faithfulness strongly'. The KJV 'merciful' leaves out the covenant sense of חסד, loyalty between two sides.
'You show yourself blameless, whole'. Ibn Ezra says the form swallows a third tav, like תִּתְחַזָּק, and that it means either 'he will see your work as whole' or 'you are whole of mind'.

'Man'. It is not the usual אִישׁ. Ibn Ezra calls it an adjective in a form that is not a construct; Radak and Metzudat Zion read it as a plain word for man, a different pattern of the same word (Prov 30:19).

verses.translation_literal: With a pure one you show yourself pure, and with a twisted one you show yourself twisted.
verses.translation_dramatic: With the pure, you are clear as water. And with the crooked, you turn out to be crooked too: every bend they take, you take it with them, and they cannot find the straight road home.
verses.directors_commentary:
The saying continues, now in its dark half. The first clause repeats the structure of verse 26 and then breaks the pattern: the 'and' that was missing between the earlier pair now appears, as if the speaker has gone to the other side of the scale. The sound play is the same, nabar / titbarar, 'ikkesh / titpattal, and the second pair is harsh to say aloud, with its clipped stops (t-t-p-t-l).

The KJV 'froward' is an archaic word, now meaning 'contrary', and it hides that both Hebrew words are physical pictures: 'ikkesh' is 'bent, warped', and the verb 'titpattal' is from the same root as the 'wrestling' of Genesis 30:8 and the 'twisted' generation of Deuteronomy 32:5 (Metzudat Zion on 18:27). The Hebrew implies a match of shapes: God turns out to be as winding as the path the person chose. Radak reads it as 'you bring on him his own twisted way'. Rashi connects the pair with Pharaoh, and the Targum with Jacob and Pharaoh (Rashi, Targum on Psalm 18:27). The parallel in 2 Samuel 22:27 has slightly different forms, as Meiri notes.

philological_notes.note: A Hithpael of 'to twist, wrestle'. The same root gives Rachel's 'naftulei Elohim' (Gen 30:8). Ibn Ezra reads it as 'you wrestle until you win', so the sense is not only 'crooked' but 'contending'.
'Bent, twisted, perverse'. Metzudat Zion glosses it as 'crooked' (akum), a physical word turned moral.

verses.translation_literal: For you, you save a poor people, and eyes uplifted you bring low.
verses.translation_dramatic: For you lift the poor and the afflicted out of their ruin, and the proud, the ones who look down over their own cheekbones, you bring low. Those high eyes will fall.
verses.directors_commentary:
'For' (ki) gives the reason for the saying of verses 26-27: God's justice is not a mere mirror but a reversal. The pronoun 'you' is stated in Hebrew, which is not needed for the verb, so it is emphatic: 'it is you, and no one else, who saves'. Play it as a turn from reflection to praise.

The KJV 'afflicted people' is acceptable, but 'people' (am) here is a word that can mean the nation as a whole, which is why Ibn Ezra comments that saving a whole people is a greater wonder than saving one man (Ibn Ezra on 18:28). 'Eyes uplifted' is KJV's 'high looks', which is good English for the Hebrew but loses the image of the eyes themselves as the organ of pride. Radak says the Bible ties eyes and sin together, as in Numbers 15:39 'do not go about after your hearts and your eyes' (Radak on 18:28). Ancient audiences knew the posture of the haughty look: the chin up, the gaze sent over the heads of others.

philological_notes.note: 'Raised eyes': pride shown by the face. Radak notes that pride and sin are tied to the eyes, quoting Numbers 15:39 and Job 31:7.
'Poor, afflicted, brought low'. It is the word the speaker will use of God's own stooping in verse 36 ('anvatkha) through the shared root, so the people God saves are the ones who are already low.

verses.translation_literal: For you, you light my lamp; YHWH my God makes bright my darkness.
verses.translation_dramatic: For it is you who lights my lamp. The LORD, my God, shines on my darkness until it gives way.
verses.directors_commentary:
The mood turns to night. A lamp in the ancient world was a small clay dish of olive oil with a wick, the only light in a house, and to let it go out was a sign of disaster (as in Proverbs 13:9). To 'light my lamp' is to give life and a future, and the word 'lamp' is also used of a royal house elsewhere (2 Samuel 21:17 calls David 'the lamp of Israel'), which suits a king. Again the Hebrew puts 'you' in front for emphasis.

KJV 'candle' is an error of its time: there were no wax candles in David's world, only oil lamps. KJV 'enlighten' also suggests learning; the Hebrew verb yagiah means 'to make bright, to give shine'. Rashi reads the verse literally, for David's night battle against Amalek (1 Sam 30:17); Radak says the darkness is distress and the light is rescue, and Metzudat David says 'you send me help' (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat David on 18:29).

philological_notes.note: 'My lamp', an oil lamp. Ibn Ezra takes it as a figure for good fortune (mazal); Radak as the rescue that follows distress.
'Makes bright': from the noun for brightness (nogah, as in Isaiah 60:3). Metzudat Zion glosses it 'cause to shine'.

verses.translation_literal: For by you I run a marauding band, and by my God I leap a wall.
verses.translation_dramatic: With you I charge into the raiders. With my God I go over a wall.
verses.directors_commentary:
Here the king is a soldier. The verbs are short and fast: 'I run', 'I leap'. Two enemies are named without any article: a 'gedud', a raiding band (the same word is used for the Amalekite raiders David chased in 1 Samuel 30), and a 'shur', the wall of a town. An audience would have pictured a fortified town on a hill: walls of rough stone and mudbrick, and a gate that cannot be forced.

KJV 'run through a troop' makes the verb sound as if it meant 'pass through', but the Hebrew is simply 'run', and the noun follows directly without a preposition, 'I run a band' (YLT: 'I run—a troop!'). Radak and Meiri give the other reading, from the root rtz 'to crush': 'I shatter a band'; the vowel would then be a different one, so I keep 'run' as the plain sense (Radak, Meiri on 18:30). The 'leap' is the Piel of dalag, which is a hurdling or bounding, a jump with a purpose. BBE 'made a way through the wall' loses the leap entirely. The Midrash, cited by Rashi and Radak, ties the verse to Joab and the capture of Jebus, and says the wall was shortened for David; that is later tradition and not in the text.

philological_notes.note: 'I run a band': a bare object without a preposition. Ibn Ezra reads 'I run after a band, as one pursues'. Radak and Meiri offer 'I crush a band' from rtz; Meiri also offers 'I run toward a band'.
'Wall'. Metzudat Zion compares Genesis 49:22 'banot tsa'adah 'ale shur', where the sense is also 'wall'. It is a different word from 'shur' as 'to look' and from the name Shur.

verses.translation_literal: The God: blameless [is] his way; the word of YHWH [is] refined; a shield he [is] to all who take refuge in him.
verses.translation_dramatic: God: his way is whole and has no flaw. The word of the LORD has been through the fire, and what is left is pure. He is a shield for everyone who runs to him for cover.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker steps back from his own story to make a statement about God, and the verse reads like a creed. It is built in three short clauses with no verbs, which in Hebrew gives it the sound of a maxim. Start with 'the God', with the article, which says 'the true God, he'.

The key image is metallurgical. 'Tseruphah' is 'refined': silver heated in a crucible until the dross rises and is skimmed off. Metzudat David puts it clearly: 'like refined silver, which has no dross' (Metzudat David on 18:31). The promise of God has been tested and nothing is left but metal. Then the metaphor shifts to war: the 'magen' is the shield, here probably the small round buckler. KJV 'buckler' is right, though it is now an archaic word, and KJV 'trust' is weaker than the Hebrew verb 'chasah', which is 'to take refuge, to run for shelter' (ASV 'take refuge'). Compare verse 3, where God is a refuge. Radak's reading is that he repays each man according to his deeds.

philological_notes.note: 'Refined, smelted': the word of a goldsmith. The same root is used of silver purified in Psalm 12:7. Rashi glosses it as 'clear', adding that God 'promises and does'.
'Those who take refuge': the verb pictures an animal or person running under cover, as under a bird's wing (Ps 17:8 is a related picture). It is more active than KJV's 'trust'.

verses.translation_literal: For who [is] God from-beside YHWH, and who [is] a rock except our God?
verses.translation_dramatic: Who else is God? Name him. Look past the LORD and there is no one standing there. Who else is a rock, a cliff to set your back against? No one, apart from our God.
verses.directors_commentary:
The 'for' is the hinge. Verses 26-31 spoke of God in the third person, as a doctrine: his way is whole, his word is refined. Now the king asks two questions in the voice of a man who already knows the answer, and the questions are really a confession of loyalty. Play them as rhetoric, not as puzzles: the pause after 'who' is where the audience supplies the answer. The 'rock' (tzur) is not a metaphor of calm; for a man who hid from Saul in the crags of Judea, a rock is a place where you are not killed.

The KJV audit: the Hebrew uses two different words for 'except', mibbal'adei and zulati, and the KJV renders both with the same 'save' ('who is God save the Lord? or who is a rock save our God?'), so the variation, and the parallelism built on it, disappears. Webster copies this; BBE flattens both into 'but'. The Hebrew pairs a compound preposition (mi-bal'adei, literally 'from apart-from') with a plain noun-form (zulati), and the second line also swaps the divine name YHWH for the shared title 'our God': the first line names the LORD, the second claims him as ours. The KJV's 'the Lord' in small capitals marks the divine name correctly, but its archaic 'save' also reads, to a modern ear, as the verb 'to rescue', which is a false echo in a psalm about salvation.

philological_notes.note: A compound preposition, 'from apart-from', meaning 'except' or 'without'. It is a different word from zulati in the next line, though both translate as 'except'. English that uses one word for both loses the Hebrew's variation.

'Rock', a cliff or crag, and hence a refuge and a stronghold. Metzudat Zion glosses it as strength (chozek). In this psalm it returns the opening 'my rock' of v. 3 and v. 32 closes the circle begun there.

verses.translation_literal: The God, the one girding me [with] strength, and he made my way blameless.
verses.translation_dramatic: It is God who ties the belt of strength around me, and who makes my road whole and clear before my feet.
verses.directors_commentary:
The answer to the question of verse 32 is stated at once: the God who has just been named. The verse has two actions: he 'girds' and he 'gives'. To gird is to bind the loins with a belt before work or battle, and in the ancient Near East a soldier who was not girded was not ready: this is why the verb sounds like preparation for a fight (Metzudat Zion: from 'azor', a belt). 'Chayil' is strength, but also an army and a fighting force, and the same word is used of a 'woman of worth'.

KJV 'girdeth me with strength' is accurate and rich in English. KJV 'maketh my way perfect' uses 'perfect' for 'tamim', which now sounds like flawlessness; here it is 'complete, without gaps'. Rashi: God took stumbling-blocks from the way. Metzudat David and Radak read it as 'not a man of mine was missing in the war'. The Hebrew is 'made my way tamim', not 'made me tamim': it is the road, not the speaker, that is whole.

philological_notes.note: 'The one who girds me': a Piel participle with the article, used as a title for God. Metzudat Zion derives it from 'azor' (belt, girdle).
'Strength, force', and also an army or wealth. Here, as the object of 'girds', it is the strength a fighter ties on.

verses.translation_literal: Making my feet like the does, and on my high places he makes me stand.
verses.translation_dramatic: He makes my feet as sure as a doe's, and sets me upright on the high ground, where no one can come at me from below.
verses.directors_commentary:
The picture is of a hind on a mountain, the quickest and surest-footed animal that a Judean audience knew. A doe leaps from rock to rock on the ledges of the hills near En-gedi, where David hid from Saul, and does not slip. The verb 'meshavveh' means 'makes level, equal, like', so the feet are made 'equal to' a doe's.

The Hebrew says 'does' in the feminine plural, which Rashi explains: the legs of the female stand straighter than the male's (Rashi on 18:34). 'High places' is 'bamot'. The same word names the open-air shrines of the Canaanite religion that the Bible condemns, but here it is the natural heights, the mountain crests, and in poetry, a place of honour and victory (Deuteronomy 32:13; Habakkuk 3:19 has this very couplet). Metzudat David takes it as 'my greatness', a metaphor of rank. KJV 'hinds' feet' is an archaic word for 'does', and 'setteth me upon my high places' is accurate. BBE 'roes' feet' makes the animal a roe deer, which is not what 'ayyalah' means.

philological_notes.note: 'Like the does': the feminine plural of 'ayyal' (deer). The same image is used in Habakkuk 3:19 and in the same psalm's parallel in 2 Samuel 22:34.
'My high places': the heights, here the mountain strongholds. Meiri reads them as 'the strong places to which I had fled', Metzudat David as 'my height and greatness'.

verses.translation_literal: Teaching my hands for the war, and a bow of bronze is bent by my arms.
verses.translation_dramatic: He teaches my hands the craft of war, and my arms bend a bow of bronze, as other men bend a green branch.
verses.directors_commentary:
The training of a soldier: hands that learn war. In an age before standing armies, a king was a fighter first, and the skill of arms was reckoned a gift from the god of battle. The line ends in an image of exaggerated strength, and the commentators argue about it, because the verb is rare.

A 'bow of bronze' is not a bow made wholly of metal; it may be a composite bow strengthened with metal, or a poetic way of saying an unbendable bow, as at Job 20:24 ('a bow of bronze'). The verb 'nichatah' is hard. Rashi says it is a word for 'drawing a bow' and that David hung bronze bows in his house to frighten kings (Rashi on 18:35). Radak and Metzudat Zion derive it from 'to break'. KJV 'a bow of steel is broken' follows that second reading; 'steel' is also wrong, since steel was not known in David's age and 'nechushah' is bronze or copper. ASV 'do bend a bow of brass' follows the first reading. I take the sense 'is bent down', with the bow as subject and the arms as agent. In Hebrew the 'arms' are named last, which keeps the weight on the strength, not on the weapon.

philological_notes.note: A disputed form. Rashi: 'drawing a bow', as in 'your arrows have come down (nichatu) on me' (Ps 38:3). Radak and Metzudat Zion: 'bring down, break'. Ibn Ezra offers two options: a root nun-chet-tav, or a Niphal with a missing letter. I read it as 'is bent down' with the bow as subject.
'Bronze, copper', not steel. Radak defines it as strong metal and compares Leviticus 26:19 ('your land like bronze').

verses.translation_literal: And you gave to me [the] shield of your salvation, and your right hand supports me, and your humility makes me great.
verses.translation_dramatic: And you, you gave me the shield, and the shield was your own saving. Your right hand holds me up when my strength has run out. And your lowering of yourself, your stooping down to me, lifts me high.
verses.directors_commentary:
After five verses about God in the third person ('the God who girded me', 'he teaches my hands'), the psalm turns again to 'you', the voice of vv. 26-28, and this verse is where the king stops describing the battle and thanks the one who won it. The three clauses go from outside to inside: a shield, a hand, a quality of God's character. Note the shield is 'the shield of your salvation': what protects him is not armor but God's act of saving.

The audit of the KJV: it has 'thy gentleness hath made me great'. The word is 'anvatkha, from the root of 'anav and 'ani, 'poor', 'bowed', 'lowly', and 'gentleness' is a soft guess at it. YLT's 'lowliness' is closer, BBE's 'mercy' is a paraphrase. The sense in Radak and Metzudat David is a divine stooping: the great God lowers himself to attend to a shepherd, and that bending raises the shepherd up. The verb is the hiphil tarbeni, 'makes me many' or 'makes me great', a verb of multiplication. For a king whose men were few against many, the numbers, not only rank, are in view. The KJV's 'holden me up' is archaic for 'supports', and the verb is imperfect, a continuing act: 'is supporting me'. Play the middle clause with the right hand: in the ancient world the right hand is the hand of strength and of oath.

philological_notes.note: 'Your humility', 'your lowliness', from the family of 'anav and 'ani ('bowed', 'poor'). Said of God it means his stooping to attend to a lesser person, not a mild temper. Rashi takes it as a measure of conduct God has multiplied toward David; Radak reads it as God lowering his own honor to look at him.
Hiphil of rabah, 'to be many', so 'to make many, make great'. Ibn Ezra relates it to rav, 'chief' (as in rav beito, 'chief of his house').

verses.translation_literal: You enlarge my step under me, and my ankles do not slip.
verses.translation_dramatic: You have widened the road beneath my feet, and my ankles do not buckle.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker is a warrior-king in full flight across rough country, and the image is of a path made roomy enough that he cannot turn his foot. In a narrow wadi or on loose scree a runner's ankle is the first thing to go; to be 'enlarged' is to have room to run. The Hebrew is concrete about the body: it says 'ankles' (קַרְסֻלַּי), a dual noun, not the vague 'feet' of KJV, which turns a specific joint into a general idea. The medieval commentators (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Meiri) read it as 'legs' or even 'knees' because the Targum translates the Hebrew of Lev 11:21 as 'ankles', but the plain word is the ankle. The same idea appears in Proverbs: 'when you walk, your step will not be cramped' (Rashi on Psalm 18:37, citing Prov 4:12). Note that KJV makes the second clause a purpose ('that my feet did not slip') where the Hebrew simply sets the two clauses side by side with 'and not'. Play it as a runner's relief, not a boast.

philological_notes.note: To make wide, to give room. The word is used elsewhere of relief from distress ('in distress you gave me room', Ps 4:2), so the 'wide step' also means freedom from being cornered.
To totter, slip, give way. Metzudat Zion defines it as 'being displaced from one's place'; Rashi glosses it with an Old French word meaning to slip.

verses.translation_literal: I pursue my enemies and I overtake them, and I do not return until their finishing.
verses.translation_dramatic: I run my enemies down. I come up with them, and I do not turn back until the last of them is finished.
verses.directors_commentary: This is the king's first-person victory recital: no hedging, no divine name in the verse, only 'I'. The verbs are a rapid pair, 'pursue' and 'overtake', the standard vocabulary of ancient warfare, where the real killing happened when a beaten army broke and ran. Practically, a routed army was cut down in the open, and the pursuit ended only when the pursuers were exhausted, so 'I do not return until' is a claim of unusual stamina. KJV smooths the repeated 'I' into 'neither did I turn again', and renders the final word 'till they were consumed'. The Hebrew form (כַּלּוֹתָם) is an infinitive with a suffix, literally 'until their finishing', where the root כלה carries 'complete, end, consume' together. Radak finds the model in David's campaign against Amalek. The tense of all these verbs is open: KJV and Webster say 'I have pursued', ASV 'I will pursue', YLT and BBE use the present. Deliver the line as a flat statement of a habit.

philological_notes.note: Infinitive construct of כלה with a suffix: 'their completion/finishing'. Means both 'until they were finished off' and 'until they came to an end'.

verses.translation_literal: I shatter them, and they are not able to rise; they fall under my feet.
verses.translation_dramatic: I break them, and they cannot get up. They go down beneath my feet.
verses.directors_commentary: The verb 'shatter' (מָחַץ) is an image of crushing a skull or a limb; Metzudat Zion links it to the verse where God 'shatters the head' (Ps 110:6), so this is no wound that heals. The enemies do not retreat; they do not get up. 'Under my feet' is the royal posture of victory in the ancient Near East: Egyptian and Mesopotamian reliefs show the king with his foot on the enemy's neck, so the verse does more than describe a battlefield, it describes a monument. KJV 'I have wounded them' is too gentle: a wound can be survived, and the Hebrew says 'shattered', and the next clause says they cannot rise. Malbim hears an escalation, in that even a small blow keeps them down, and then they fall of their own accord. Let the actor spit the word 'shatter' and then go very quiet on 'they cannot rise'.

philological_notes.note: To smash, strike through, crush. Stronger than 'wound': the same root is used of smashing a head (Ps 110:6) and of shattering a limb.

verses.translation_literal: And you girded me [with] strength for the battle; you make bow down those who rise against me under me.
verses.translation_dramatic: You belted me with strength, and the strength was meant for war. And those who stood up against me, you bent their knees, and they sank beneath me.
verses.directors_commentary:
This verse closes the battle sequence by returning to its beginning. Verse 33 said 'the God who girded me with strength'; here the same verb, 'azar, comes back in the second person, and the same word chayil ('strength', also 'army' and 'valor'). Soldiers girded their loins by tying the long robe up into a belt before they fought, so 'girding' is the action of readiness, not of armor. The enemies are named by a participle of qum, 'those who rise up against me' (qamai), and this answers the previous verse's 'not able to rise' (v. 39), where the same verb qum appeared: those who stood up against the king cannot stand up again. A listener hears the root twice in a few breaths.

The KJV audit: 'thou hast subdued under me' for takhria' is a weakened rendering. The verb is kara', 'to kneel, to bow down, to sink on the knees', the word used of a man buckling; Metzudat Zion says it means falling on the knees, and Meiri that the enemies become like those who cannot walk. The KJV's 'subdued' is a political word and does not show the physical picture. The final 'under me' (tachtai) sounds the third in a series that began in vv. 37 and 39: the king's feet and the enemies beneath them.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of kara', 'to bow, kneel, sink down on the knees'. The causative makes enemies kneel or collapse. 'Subdued' loses the body.
A participle of qum, 'those who rise against me'. It echoes the 'not able to rise' of v. 39, so the verse is joined to the previous one by the same root.

verses.translation_literal: And my enemies, you give me [the] neck, and those who hate me, I destroy them.
verses.translation_dramatic: My enemies you turn from me, and all I see is the back of their necks. And those who hated me, I cut them off.
verses.directors_commentary: The speaker's picture is of a fleeing army, and what the victor sees is the nape of the neck. 'To give the neck' is a Hebrew idiom for turning one's back in flight, and every medieval commentator in the packet says so (Rashi, Radak, Meiri, Metzudat David). Ibn Ezra points to Genesis 49:8, 'your hand will be on the neck of your enemies'. KJV 'Thou hast also given me the necks of mine enemies' is a literal calque that sounds as if God had handed over heads for execution; ASV and BBE recover the sense of 'turning their backs'. Note the grammar: the first half is a fronted object ('my enemies, you gave me the neck'), and the second half switches from 'you' to 'I'; the king is the one who finishes the job. 'Destroy' (אַצְמִיתֵם) is the root of 'cutting off': Metzudat Zion links it to Psalm 101, 'I will cut off'.

philological_notes.note: The back of the neck, the nape. 'To give the nape' means that the enemy turns his back in flight, so that the pursuer sees only the neck; the opposite of 'stiff-necked' (קְשֵׁה עֹרֶף) which means refusing to turn.
Hiphil of צמת, to silence or cut off completely.

verses.translation_literal: They cry for help, and there is no deliverer; to YHWH, and he does not answer them.
verses.translation_dramatic: They cry out for help, and no one comes to save them. They cry even to the LORD, and he does not answer.
verses.directors_commentary: A silence falls on the battlefield. The enemies who were running now beg, first for any rescuer, and then, in the most awkward turn of the psalm, to YHWH himself. In the ancient Near East a defeated army would appeal to its own gods or to an ally; here the king is claiming that even the God of Israel will not take their side, and the wording is chosen to shock. 'They cry for help' uses the verb שָׁוַע, the desperate shout of someone with no other resort, not the formal word for prayer. KJV 'even unto the Lord' puts words in italics for 'even', because the Hebrew simply says 'to YHWH'; and it prints 'Lord', not the divine name. The preposition is also odd: עַל, 'on/upon', is used for אֶל, 'to', as Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri note, citing Hannah's prayer in 1 Samuel 1:10 (ותתפלל על יהוה). Rashi reads it differently, that the first cry is to their own idols and only afterwards to YHWH; Radak adds that their hearts were not sincere. Play the last clause as a door shut.

philological_notes.note: Piel: to cry out for help; a cry from someone with no other recourse, not liturgical prayer.
'Upon YHWH' used for 'to YHWH': עַל stands for אֶל, as in 1 Sam 1:10.

verses.translation_literal: And I crush them like dust on the face of [the] wind; like [the] mud of [the] streets I pour them out.
verses.translation_dramatic: I grind them down to dust and the wind takes it from its face. Like the mud of the streets I tip them out.
verses.directors_commentary: Two images follow, one of the dry season and one of the wet. In summer the road is fine dust, and a gust lifts it off the ground ('on the face of the wind', as the Hebrew has it, an image of the whole surface of the air); in winter the same street is mud. The enemy is first ground to powder, then emptied out like slops, and the contempt is the point. Both images were literal: the narrow lanes of an Iron Age town were beaten earth, unpaved, with sewage and rubbish tipped into them. KJV 'beat them small as the dust' is close, but 'cast them out as the dirt in the streets' misses the verb: the Hebrew is 'pour out, empty', the word for emptying a jar. The ultimate image is of vessels being drained. Rashi cites the verb's use in Genesis 42:35, where men 'empty their sacks', and Jeremiah 48:11, 'not emptied from vessel to vessel'. Radak and Meiri debate whether the root is ריק 'empty' or רקק 'spittle, mire'. Either way the picture is of a man disposing of rubbish.

philological_notes.note: To pound or grind fine, as in the incense of Exodus 30:36. Not the verb for laughter, although the same consonants.
Hiphil: to empty out, pour out; used of emptying sacks and vessels. Some medievals (Radak, Meiri) derive it from רקק, 'spittle, mire', which gives the same picture.

verses.translation_literal: You deliver me from [the] strivings of a people; you set me as head of nations; a people I have not known serve me.
verses.translation_dramatic: You lift me out of the strife of a people, and set me at the head of nations. A people I never knew come to serve me.
verses.directors_commentary: The tone changes from battle to politics. The king's rise was not only military: 'strivings' (רִיבֵי) is the word for quarrels, lawsuits and civil strife, and the commentators read it as the dispute inside Israel: Saul's faction, Absalom's revolt (Ibn Ezra, Radak). The parallel in 2 Samuel 22:44 has 'my people' (עַמִּי), so some understand it that way. Meiri and Metzudat David think foreign wars are meant. KJV 'the heathen' for גּוֹיִם is a loaded word: the Hebrew just says 'nations'. 'Head of nations' is what ancient texts call an overlord whose vassals send tribute; Radak points to Edom and Aram, who were David's servants (2 Sam 8:6, 14). 'A people I did not know' is a claim of reach: states he never met, far enough away that he had no dealings with them (Metzudat David). The final verb is imperfect: 'they serve me' as a continuing arrangement, which KJV renders 'shall serve me' as a promise.

philological_notes.note: Strife, quarrel, dispute at law or in arms. Whether the 'people' are Israel in revolt or foreign nations is disputed.
'To be head of nations' means being overlord, with vassals paying tribute. Radak names Edom and Aram.

verses.translation_literal: At [the] hearing of an ear they are heard by me; sons of foreignness lie to me.
verses.translation_dramatic: The moment a rumor reaches their ears, they obey me. The sons of strangers cringe and lie to my face.
verses.directors_commentary: The first clause is a pun in sound: לְשֵׁמַע אֹזֶן יִשָּׁמְעוּ, 'at the hearing of an ear they are heard', the same root שמע twice. It means they obey at a mere report, with no need for an army to be sent. KJV gets the sense with 'as soon as they hear of me', but loses the repetition of the root. Radak and Meiri cite David's reputation after the Aramean war (2 Sam 8:13). The second clause is stranger. 'Sons of foreignness' (בְּנֵי נֵכָר) is the common idiom for foreigners; the verb יְכַחֲשׁוּ means to lie, deceive, or feign. KJV 'shall submit themselves' and ASV 'foreigners shall submit' smooth it into plain obedience; YLT 'feign obedience' and BBE 'with false hearts' are closer. The verse is saying that their obedience was a mask of fear: Rashi says 'out of fear', Metzudat David 'they speak lies, saying they love me, because they fear me'. For an actor it is a chilling line: the king knows he is lied to, and accepts it.

philological_notes.note: 'At the hearing of an ear', an idiom for hearing by report; the root שמע is then repeated in יִשָּׁמְעוּ, 'they are heard / they obey'.
Piel: to lie, deceive, feign, or cringe. The obedience described is outward and forced.

verses.translation_literal: Sons of foreignness wither, and they come trembling out of their strongholds.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sons of strangers wilt like leaves, and they come out of their fortresses shaking.
verses.directors_commentary: The foreigners are in their fortified refuges and are afraid to leave them. 'Wither' (יִבֹּלוּ) is the word for a leaf that dries up and falls, so the picture is of men drained of colour and strength by fear (Radak: 'like a withering leaf'). The second verb (וְיַחְרְגוּ) is a puzzle: it is found only here, and the old tradition gives it two meanings. The Targum and Ibn Ezra and Radak, citing Deuteronomy 32:25, take it as 'tremble'; Rashi cites alternative readings, 'be loosened', or 'limp like shackled men', and Malbim 'come limping from the long journey'. KJV 'be afraid out of their close places' and ASV 'come trembling' follow the first reading, YLT 'are slain' follows neither. 'Close places' in KJV is an archaism for מִסְגְּרוֹת, fortified enclosures, closed-in places. In a world of walled cities and hill-fortresses, to come out of the fortress is to surrender. In 2 Samuel 22:46 the verb is spelled differently (ויחגרו). Say the line with the breath going out of it.

philological_notes.note: To fade, wilt, wither, as a leaf. Rashi also reads it as 'be weary', citing Exodus 18:18.
A rare verb, only here. The oldest tradition takes it as 'tremble' (Targum on Deut 32:25); others as 'limp' or 'be loosened'. The parallel in 2 Samuel 22:46 reads differently.
From סגר, 'to shut': enclosures, strongholds, places where one is shut in; Ibn Ezra says 'their lofty palaces', Rashi 'prison-cells'.

verses.translation_literal: [As] YHWH lives! And blessed [is] my rock, and exalted be [the] God of my salvation.
verses.translation_dramatic: The LORD lives! Blessed be my Rock, and may he be lifted high, the God who saves me.
verses.directors_commentary: After the long battle recital the speech breaks into a cry of worship. 'YHWH lives' (חַי־יְהוָה) is the formula of an oath ('as YHWH lives'), but here it is a plain acclamation: in a world of gods of wood and stone, the living God is the claim itself. Meiri reads it exactly so: unlike the idols who 'have a mouth but cannot speak' (Ps 115:5), this God is alive. KJV 'The Lord liveth' is accurate, but the capitalised 'Lord' replaces the name; the Hebrew has YHWH. 'Rock' (צוּר) is the central image of the psalm, a place of refuge in the broken hill country where the king hid (Ps 18:2), and Metzudat Zion glosses it 'my strength'. The verbs switch between statement ('blessed is') and wish ('may he be exalted', יָרוּם). KJV makes both wishes ('blessed be my rock; and let the God... be exalted') while the first has no verb and could be either. Note the word play of 'Rock' and 'exalted': the Rock is the high place.

philological_notes.note: The formula of an oath, 'as YHWH lives', used here as an exclamation of praise; in the mouths of the gods' worshippers it would be an empty claim.
'My rock': a cliff or crag where one takes refuge. Metzudat Zion reads it as 'my strength'.

verses.translation_literal: The God who gives vengeance to me, and he drives peoples under me.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the God who gives me vengeance, and brings whole peoples to heel under me.
verses.directors_commentary: The climax names the God, and the credit lies where the king has put it throughout: even his own vengeance is a gift. 'Vengeance' (נְקָמוֹת) is plural, 'acts of vengeance', and in Hebrew law the word is not petty spite but the right of a legitimate authority to set wrongs right; Rashi hears it as God giving the king 'strength to take vengeance'. KJV 'It is God that avengeth me' makes God the avenger in the king's place, which turns the Hebrew phrase, 'who gives vengeances to me', into something quieter. The second verb is a real puzzle. וַיַּדְבֵּר is from דבר, which in the hiphil is 'to drive, lead' (as a shepherd drives a flock, Ex 3:1), though some readers (Rashi first, and Radak's second option) connect it to דֶּבֶר, 'plague'. The Hebrew picture is of peoples herded under the king, as a drover moves sheep, which is why the Targum (וּדְבַר) and Meiri read it as 'led'; KJV 'subdueth' flattens that into an abstract word. Play it as a drover's image, with 'under me' falling at the end like a gate closing.
