philological_notes.note: Plural, 'acts of vengeance'; the right to set a wrong right, not spite.
Hiphil of דבר, 'to drive, lead' (as in Ex 3:1 and Ps 47:4). Rashi also offers 'kill' (from דֶּבֶר, plague); Radak and Meiri 'lead them from their place and put them under me'.

verses.translation_literal: My deliverer from my enemies, also from those who rise against me you lift me up, from a man of violence you rescue me.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the one who slips me free of my enemies. More than that: above the very ones who stood up against me, you set me high. And from the man of violence, the man of violence, you pull me out.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice is a king at the end of a long song, and he speaks in two tenses at once: a participle ("my deliverer") and two imperfects ("you lift me up, you rescue me"). Play it as habit and experience, not a single rescue. The sentence also turns from talking about God to talking to him, mid-line, and the actor should let that shift happen in the breath.

KJV keeps "He delivereth" and then "thou hast delivered", which flattens the repeated rescue into past completion and blurs the participle's "my deliverer". It also smooths the Hebrew "from a man of violence" into "the violent man", but chamas is a heavy word: not mere roughness but injustice by force, bloodshed and wrong. Note the word play of rising: those who "rise" (qamai) against him are met by God who makes him "rise" (teromemeni), the same movement reversed.

The tradition splits on the "man of violence". Radak and Meiri say Saul, Ibn Ezra allows a Philistine king or Saul. The text itself leaves him a single unnamed figure after a plural, which sharpens the menace.

philological_notes.note: Violence as wrong done by force, injustice that harms the weak; stronger than 'violent' as an adjective in English. Here in a construct, 'a man of violence'.
Those who 'rise' (qum) against me are answered by 'you raise me' (rum). The sound and the motion answer each other; the same root of height recurs through the psalm.

verses.translation_literal: Upon so, I will thank you among the nations, YHWH, and to your name I will make music.
verses.translation_dramatic: And so, LORD, I will lift my voice where all can hear it. Out among the nations I will thank you, and your name will be the song I sing.
verses.directors_commentary:
Al-ken, "upon so," is a hinge: everything the king has just said, the rescue from enemies and the setting on high, is the reason for what comes next. Radak glosses it "because you did all these things for me" (Radak on Psalm 18:50), and Metzudat David "because of this great deliverance." Play it as a conclusion reached, not a new thought.

The weight falls on "among the nations." Radak reads it as the king thanking God before every people that hears of him and serves him; Meiri reads it as making the thanks known publicly to everyone (Meiri on Psalm 18:50). This is a victor whose subjects include foreigners, and he will not keep the credit for himself: Radak adds that the strength is the LORD's, not his. The Hebrew verb for thanks, odeh, is public by nature: it is acknowledgment spoken aloud, not a private feeling. The second verb, azammerah, is singing to an instrument, music made for the name.

KJV audit: "the heathen" is an archaizing, judgmental word; Hebrew goyim is simply "nations," the neutral word for peoples, and the ASV and BBE are closer. "Sing praises" is fair, though it hides that zamar is the verb of making music. The Hebrew leaves the divine name as YHWH where the KJV has "Lord" in small capitals. Paul quotes this line in Romans 15:9 to show that the nations were always meant to hear God praised.

philological_notes.note: From yadah, to acknowledge or confess, hence to thank in public. The thanks is spoken before an audience, which is why 'among the nations' fits it. YLT's 'confess' keeps the sense of open acknowledgment; Radak ties it to making known before all peoples.
'Among the nations': the non-Israelite peoples. The KJV 'heathen' adds a verdict the word does not carry. Radak understands the nations as those who hear of the king and serve him.

verses.translation_literal: Making great the victories of his king, and doing covenant loyalty to his anointed, to David and to his offspring, until perpetuity.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the one who makes great the victories of his king. He keeps faith with the one he anointed, with David, and with David's children after him, on and on, without end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends by changing person: the king stops speaking to God and speaks about him, in two participles, "making great" and "doing," which present God's care as continuing. It is the closing line of a song of a king, and it ends with the king's own name, David, spoken in the third person, as a signature. Radak says the king speaks of himself here, as "his king" and "his anointed" (Radak on Psalm 18:51).

The key word is chesed, covenant loyalty. It is a bond that binds the stronger party, not a favor. Metzudat David stresses that this deliverance comes "not as payment but as chesed," and Malbim ties it to the promise made to David that kingship would not leave his line, which he calls grace (Malbim on Psalm 18:51, citing 2 Samuel 7). That is why the verse reaches forward: "his offspring, until perpetuity." Radak: as he made his deliverances great and did him chesed, so he will do for his seed forever. Meiri hears in the last verses a prophecy for the days of the Messiah, with "his anointed" meaning the king Messiah (Meiri on Psalm 18:51). Actors should know the line can bear that reading, and that the Hebrew word mashiach simply means "anointed one," a king set apart by oil.

The text carries a written and a read form: the consonants say magdil, "making great," and the marginal reading is migdol, "tower of," the form in 2 Samuel 22:51. Radak says the two are the same sense: migdol there is a descriptive form, and Meiri hears a play on the "tower" of victories. KJV audit: "great deliverance giveth he" bends the order and turns a participle into a finite verb; "sheweth mercy" softens chesed into pity, when the word means loyalty owed within a covenant; "his seed" is literal but archaic for zera', offspring.

philological_notes.note: Covenant loyalty, faithful commitment, more than the mercy of the KJV. Malbim reads it as the grace of the promise that kingship would not depart from David's line, and as lasting forever.
Written as the causative participle 'making great'; read as migdol, the form of 2 Samuel 22:51. Radak holds both forms to carry one sense; Metzudat Zion explains it as from the root of 'great'.
'To his anointed': the king set apart by anointing. Meiri also hears the end of the song as pointing to the days of the Messiah.
